about: Sizes of a man's hand for fitting the drawn hand of "Shape, by gradient descent" to the deck's reference hand, the ANSUR II men's mean (193.3 mm). Written by RA, 2026-11-09, for the drawing agent. Lengths in mm. Each outside dimension carries its survey, page, n, mean, SD, the survey's own definition, how many separately worded reads of the primary agreed (reads), and its value scaled to the reference hand. recommended_targets holds one value per dimension. Provisional or unverified values say so in their note or status.

scaling.rule: value x (193.28 / the survey's mean hand length) for lengths; value x (88.26 / the survey's mean hand breadth) for breadths, depths and thicknesses
scaling.recommendation: Use the scaled values (scaled_to_reference_mm, and recommended_targets). Greiner's hands are 0.4 % longer than the reference and Garrett's 2.0 % longer: scaling moves Greiner's figures by under 1 mm and Garrett's by up to 4 mm (its fingertip heights).

how_to_measure_the_model: Lay the hand flat, palm down, fingers straight and together as far as they go, thumb held out. Draw the wrist-crease baseline: the line across the palm side at the distal wrist crease (through its ulnar and radial ends), square to the middle finger.
Heights are perpendicular to that baseline; tip-to-wrist-crease lengths run along each digit's own axis to the baseline; crotch heights go to the deepest point of each web.

Hand length: baseline (stylion level) to the middle fingertip. Hand breadth: across the outermost points of the index and little fingers' knuckle joints, thumb out of the way. Hand thickness: back to palm at the middle finger's knuckle.
Joint breadths and depths: the greatest breadth (side to side) and depth (back to pad) at each joint, finger free, not pressed flat.

not_found.hand_breadth_across_the_thumb: Not in Greiner 1991 or Garrett 1970. White 1980 (NATICK/TR-81/010, "hand breadth at thumb", measured at the thumb's first joint) has it, but its tables were unreadable in the scan.
not_found.hand_thickness_in_ansur: ANSUR II and Greiner did not measure hand thickness; Garrett 1970 is the source.
not_found.fingertip_and_nail_sizes: Not re-read in this pass. The film's finger (deck/src/06-motion.js) records, unverified here: AIST Japanese men (Kouchi 2012, n 327) index breadth at the tip joint 15.6, at mid-nail 13.9, depth at the tip joint 13.0, nail base to fingertip 14.2, nail breadth 10.9; thumb joint breadth 20.1, depth 17.3, nail base to tip 15.7, nail breadth 14.7; Ha et al. 2015 men's index nail 12.3 wide x 13.0 long, thumb 15.2 x 14.7. Against these, U.S. Air Force men measure 18.4 mm across and 15.5 mm deep at the index's tip joint and 22.9 by 20.2 at the thumb's (Garrett 1970, above): the Japanese figures are about 15 % slimmer.

links_between_joint_centres_mm.for_the_drawing: The whole first bone is 46 to 49 mm between its joint surfaces, but the base joint turns about a centre inside the bone's near end, so between joint centres the first link is 36 to 39 mm. A model whose thumb joints are joint centres should have a first link of about 37 mm, not 46.9: stretching it to 46.9 makes the thumb about 10 mm too long and pushes it outward.

39.rests_on: K.-S. Lee and M.-C. Jung, "Flexion and Extension Angles of Resting Fingers and Wrist", Int. J. Occupational Safety and Ergonomics 20(1):91-101 (2014), Table 3, forearm neutral: 39 (SD 12), 40 relaxed hands (20 men, 20 women), 4 mm markers on the skin of the back of the thumb, Vicon. The paper does not say what line the angle is measured from.

25.rests_on: 39 less the over-read of skin markers, 6 to 24 deg, which gives 15 to 33 deg; 25 is near its middle. How the over-read was got: marker_over_read below.

12.5.rests_on: W. P. Cooney III, M. J. Lucca, E. Y. S. Chao and R. L. Linscheid, "The kinesiology of the thumb trapeziometacarpal joint", J. Bone Joint Surg. 63-A(9):1371-1381 (1981): the rest position of their 19 adults (9 men, 10 women, mean age 26) is described as the thumb against the thumb side of the index finger's end bone, as for a key pinch, with the knuckle and the tip joint each flexed 10 to 15 deg. No mean, no SD, no table: it describes the pose, it is not a result. Only the base joint was measured at rest, from metal markers taped to the skin and seen on two-plane X-rays.

tip_joint_deg.rests_on: Lee & Jung 2014, Table 3: 10 (SD 6), 40 hands, skin markers. M. S. Rogers, A. B. Barr, B. Kasemsontitum and D. M. Rempel, "A three-dimensional anthropometric solid model of the hand based on landmark measurements", Ergonomics 51(4):511-526 (2008), Table 4, 100 hands, landmarks on the palm side: 6.0 (SD 14.8) relaxed round a large ball, 17.1 (SD 16.2) holding a mouse. Cooney 1981 describes 10 to 15.

first_bone_on_the_trapezium.source: Cooney et al. 1981, Table III, rest position; from skin-taped markers on two-plane X-rays

markers.source: Lee & Jung 2014, Table 3, "CMC"; what it is measured from is not stated (most likely the first bone's tilt out of the plane of the palm)

marker_over_read.fingers_source: J. R. Cook, N. A. Baker, R. Cham, E. Hale and M. S. Redfern, "Measurements of wrist and finger postures: a comparison of goniometric and motion capture techniques", J. Appl. Biomech. 23(1):70-78 (2007), Table 2: 5 people, 4 mm markers; at about 30 deg the markers read the index knuckle 4.1 deg (SD 4.6) and the middle knuckle 4.6 deg (SD 4.8) more flexed than a goniometer; the middle joints within 2 deg.
marker_over_read.thumb_status: ESTIMATE by geometry, not a measurement
marker_over_read.how: A marker sits on the skin, above the bone. The line from one marker to the next is not the bone's line when the two markers stand at different heights above the bones' axes. Heights taken: thumb knuckle 14 mm (half of a knuckle about 24 mm deep, plus the marker's 2 mm), tip joint 12 mm (half of 20.2 mm, Garrett 1970, plus 2). Across the second link (35 mm) the marker line drops atan(2 / 35) = 3 deg. Across the first link (37 mm) it rises atan((14 - h) / 37), h the height of the "virtual marker" at the thumb's base, which the paper does not give: 21 deg if it sits at the joint's centre (h 0), 3 deg if at skin height (h 12). A straight thumb would then read 6 to 24 deg bent at the knuckle.

holding_a_mouse.source: Rogers et al. 2008 (above); 100 hands of mean length 178.1 mm

where_the_tip_lies.cooney_1981: the thumb's pulp against the thumb side of the index's end bone, at its middle (a posed rest)
where_the_tip_lies.derived_for_the_studys_hand: With the fingers at the study's rest angles (index 29 / 29 / 10 deg), links 37 / 35 / 32 mm and the base 56 mm behind, 11.5 mm toward the palm and 5 mm toward the thumb side of the index knuckle, the thumb's skin tip reaches the thumb side of the index's MIDDLE bone: about half-way along it with the knuckle at 12.5 deg, two-fifths with 25 deg, one-fifth with 39 deg. It does not reach the index's end bone unless the fingers are curled more (40 deg or more at their knuckles).

relaxed.for_the_slide_source_line: Thumb knuckle: 39 deg, Lee & Jung 2014 (skin markers, 40 hands; reference line not defined); 10 to 15 deg as described for the resting thumb by Cooney et al. 1981 (not measured). Thumb tip joint: 10 deg, Lee & Jung 2014; 6 deg and 17 deg in Rogers et al. 2008 (100 hands).
